summary:
Planet Pulse is a concept for an interactive sonification experience that turns NASA Earth science data into synchronized sound. Users choose a data layer (temperature, oceans, atmosphere, ice or vegetation), watch a NASA visualization, and hear the data as audio. Temperature anomalies map to pitch, ocean measurements to flowing rhythm, ice changes to evolving texture, and vegetation to pulse and density. A legend ties each sound to its scientific meaning.

It addresses the challenge of making Earth data creative and accessible by letting people hear patterns, not just read charts. The flagship demo is a 60-second “Temperature Symphony” built on a historical NASA temperature dataset such as GISTEMP. Its core rule is that every sound must trace back to a real data value, so the result stays scientifically grounded.

It matters because it adds an audio route into science for people who can’t easily use visual charts. It also helps students explore abstract patterns, and it gives the public a memorable way to connect with climate and Earth change.
details:
What it does and how it works

Planet Pulse is a web experience that turns NASA Earth science data into sound. The user picks a data layer and presses play. A line chart draws year by year while a tone rises and falls with the values. Each year’s value is normalized and mapped to a pitch between 220 Hz and 880 Hz (two octaves). A legend explains the mapping, and reference buttons let users hear the lowest and highest pitches first. The current prototype has two working layers: global temperature anomalies and Arctic sea ice. The planned flagship demo is a 60-second “Temperature Symphony.” Oceans, atmosphere and vegetation are designed but not built yet.

Benefits

  • It gives people who can’t easily read visual charts an audio way into the data.
  • It makes abstract trends easier to explore and discuss in classrooms.
  • It helps listeners notice rises, dips and rhythms over time.
  • Every sound traces back to a real data value, so it stays explainable.

Intended impact

Our aim is for people to explain what a sound represents and trace it back to the data. We want to make climate and Earth data more inclusive, memorable and engaging for students, educators and the public. Sonification adds to visual data and doesn’t replace it.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single web page
  • Web Audio API (oscillators and filters) to generate the sound
  • HTML Canvas for the animated chart
  • NASA GISTEMP (temperature) and NSIDC (sea ice) as the data sources
  • Claude (Anthropic’s AI assistant) helped build the prototype. Add your team’s own tools here, plus any design software you used for the slide deck.
  • No special hardware: any device with a browser and speakers or headphones

What makes it creative

It is “not music inspired by Earth, but music mapped from Earth’s data.” Each layer has its own sound character, and the sea ice mapping is deliberately flipped so that losing ice raises the pitch. The Earth Data DJ console idea makes exploring feel playful while the science stays visible.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: the mappings are transparent and labeled as proposed. The prototype’s values are approximate, interpolated from published trends, so the official data series must replace them before any scientific claim.
  • Accessibility: a keyboard-friendly timeline slider and a visual display alongside the audio.
  • Listening comfort: a moderate pitch range, soft tones and a gentle start and stop.
  • Scope: start with one dataset and one mapping, then expand to more Earth systems.
  • Validation: user testing for clarity, accessibility and scientific interpretation.
